Every model in this family from VG08 onward gives each child a **constant** offset from the population trajectory: a child who is 30 words ahead at two years is assumed to be the same distance ahead, on the model's scale, at six. VG19 relaxes that. Each child gets a **rate** as well as an offset, so a child can pull away from the population curve, or drift toward it, as they grow.

![The model graph. VG19 differs from VG10 by replacing each child's single offset with an offset and a rate.](gp_model_graph.svg){#fig-graph .lightbox fig-align="left"}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Terms specific to this model"}

**Offset and rate**

: Each child carries two numbers per outcome instead of one: an offset, how far their curve sits from the population trajectory at the reference age, and a rate, how fast that distance changes per year of age. Under a constant offset every child's curve is parallel to the population's; under a rate the curves fan, converge and can cross.

**Reference age**

: The age at which the offset is read — the pool's median age — so that the offset and the rate do not trade off against each other in the sampler, and so that $\tau_0$ is a spread at a stated age rather than an extrapolation to age zero.

**Offset–rate correlation ($\rho_{01}$)**

: Whether children who sit above the population curve at the reference age also tend to pull further away from it (positive) or to drift back towards it (negative). Estimated separately for each outcome; it lives on $(-1, 1)$ with prior mass on both sides of zero, so its interval does carry evidence about its sign.

:::

## Statistical model

VG10 gives child $i$ two numbers, one on the comprehension logit and one on the logit of the production ratio $q$, and holds each fixed across that child's whole observed span. VG19 replaces each with a pair — an offset and a rate:

$$
\text{shift}_i(a) = b_{0,i} + b_{1,i} \cdot \frac{a - a_{\text{ref}}}{12}
$$

with $(b_0, b_1)$ drawn jointly per child:

$$
\begin{pmatrix} b_0 \\ b_1 \end{pmatrix} \sim
\mathcal{N}\left( \mathbf{0}, \begin{pmatrix} \tau_0^2 & \rho_{01}\tau_0\tau_1 \\ \rho_{01}\tau_0\tau_1 & \tau_1^2 \end{pmatrix} \right)
$$

Four things about this are deliberate.

**The model of record is nested at $\tau_1 = 0$.** At that value every child's rate is zero and the shift is a constant offset — VG10, op for op. The nesting is exact, but it does **not** make $\tau_1$'s own interval a test of it. $\tau_1$ carries a `HalfNormal` prior, so its posterior is supported on $(0, \infty)$ and an equal-tailed interval must exclude zero — even if the posterior is the prior and the data have said nothing. Whether children differ in their own rate of growth is a question for subject-level predictive comparison against VG10, for a formulation that puts prior mass at the point $\tau_1 = 0$, or for a practically-negligible threshold calibrated by simulation. What this parameter's interval reports is the *magnitude* of the rate spread given that the model contains one.

**$\tau_1$ is per year.** In logit per month the fitted values are around 0.02 and a prior on that scale is unreadable; per year they are 0.12 to 0.29.

**$\tau_0$ is the spread at a stated age, not at age zero.** $a_{\text{ref}}$ is 36 months, the pool's median age. Centring at the design's centre is what stops the offset and the rate trading off against each other in the sampler, and it makes $\tau_0$ a quantity with a meaning rather than an extrapolation.

**Both outcomes carry a rate, because the evidence that motivated one cannot say which curve owns it.** Gate 1 measured the drift on the *spoken proportion*, and spoken is $p_U \cdot q$: a child drifting upward there is equally consistent with drifting on comprehension, on conversion, or on both, so putting the rate on one curve alone would assume the answer. The likelihood itself is less confounded than that measurement was. On a paired row $U$ observes $p_U$ and $S \mid U$ observes $q$ separately, and only the spoken observations that take the marginal fallback branch — those with no usable comprehension count, or more words spoken than understood; the branch rows of the calibration table count them — see the product alone. So expect the two $\tau_1$ values to be correlated and individually less well resolved than the drift they jointly imply on spoken, but not structurally unidentified.

### Why a slope, and not something else

The structure was chosen before any of it was written, by fitting three candidates to the fitted residuals by maximum likelihood against a known per-observation binomial sampling variance (`notes/202608141600-rank-stability-tracking.md` §10.3). As $2\,\Delta \log L$ over a constant intercept:

| structure | spoken, all 767 | spoken, repeats 334 | understood, all 610 | understood, repeats 253 |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| random slope | 36.05 | 20.81 | 27.09 | 0.82 |
| cost of pinning $\rho_{01} = 1$ | −1.49 | −6.28 | −2.56 | −0.32 |
| AR(1) transient | no gain | — | no gain | — |

: Read as magnitudes. Both comparisons put the null on a boundary — $\tau_1 = 0$ is a variance component at zero, where $\rho_{01}$ is additionally unidentified, and $\rho_{01} = 1$ is a correlation at its own — so no chi-square reference distribution applies and no degrees of freedom are quoted. `scripts/experiments/rank_stability.py --bootstrap N` supplies a valid one by simulating under each null on the study's own design, and it has been run on the repeats-only production fit at 250 replicates. Both conclusions stand and both simulated nulls are lighter than their nominal chi-square: the slope statistic of 20.81 is beyond **every** replicate, against a null 99th percentile of 7.36, and the $\rho_{01} = 1$ statistic of 6.28 sits above a 99th percentile of 5.91. Read them as magnitudes rather than as p-values — 250 replicates cannot resolve the first below 0.004, and only two reached the second, giving an 89% Monte Carlo interval of [0.002, 0.022] ([#233](https://github.com/dseinternational/vocabulary-growth/issues/233), [`notes/202608241730`](../../../notes/202608241730-boundary-comparisons-bootstrap.md)).

Three readings, and each shaped the specification. The mean-reverting alternative **collapsed to zero persistence** on both outcomes, so what is missing is drift and not an autocorrelated child process. The spoken slope **survives restriction to children with repeated measures**, so it is genuine within-child drift rather than cross-sectional widening. And comprehension shows the opposite pattern — 27.09 across everyone, 0.82 across repeaters — so its widening looks cross-sectional, and the model must be able to represent both cases and let each outcome decide.

Pinning $\rho_{01} = 1$ leaves one deviate scaled by an age function — a rank-one covariance. It is **not** Proposal A1, although the two are easily conflated. A1 scales by $\tau_{\text{young}}\exp(\lambda t)$, which is strictly positive at every age, and holds the paired $\kappa$ constant besides; this special case scales by the affine $\tau_0 + \tau_1 D$, which vanishes at $D = -\tau_0/\tau_1$ and changes sign beyond it. They share rank-one covariance and nothing else. The difference is visible in the behaviour usually quoted for A1: under a strictly positive scale children can never cross, whereas under the affine one every child coincides at the zero and their ordering inverts past it. Pinning $\rho_{01} = 1$ costs 6.28 on 1 df on the repeats-only production fit, so it is free here.

## Priors {#sec-priors}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
from vocab_growth.report_cells import render_priors_table

render_priors_table()
```

$\tau_0$ keeps VG10's own prior on both outcomes, so the offset is unchanged and the model is one-factor against its parent. $\tau_1 \sim \text{HalfNormal}(0.5)$ has median 0.34 per year, covering both maximum-likelihood values comfortably while keeping mass near zero, so a rate the data do not support shrinks away rather than being asserted. The correlation uses $(\rho_{01}+1)/2 \sim \text{Beta}(2,2)$, which for a $2 \times 2$ matrix is exactly LKJ(2) — a gentle pull toward zero, against a maximum-likelihood value of $+0.43$ to compare with.

## Prior predictive checks {#sec-prior-predictive}

![Words understood drawn from the prior alone, before any data.](prior_samples_u.png){#fig-prior-u .lightbox fig-align="left"}

![Words spoken drawn from the prior alone.](prior_samples_s.png){#fig-prior-s .lightbox fig-align="left"}

![The production ratio drawn from the prior alone.](prior_samples_q.png){#fig-prior-q .lightbox fig-align="left"}

This is the check that matters most for this model, and it is a stiffer test than for VG10. A linear-in-age rate on the logit scale, extrapolated across an 8-115 month domain, is a strong assumption at the ends. At one prior standard deviation a child at 115 months sits well above the population trajectory **before** the offset is counted at all. What the figures have to show is that the prior admits the range of vocabularies real children have without putting appreciable mass on trajectories no child could follow.

### The child effects, which the three figures above do not contain

Those three set every random effect to zero, so they test the mean function and nothing else — which is the right check for the trend and the GP, and useless for the prior this model was added for. The figures below fill that gap (they carry no count noise either; these do). Both are computed from the same prior draws, so nothing is added to the model graph ([#233](https://github.com/dseinternational/vocabulary-growth/issues/233)).

![Individual child trajectories around a **fixed** population curve, varying only the child effect. Holding the trend fixed is what makes this readable: with a different trend under every child the curves would cross whatever the child block did, and a rate could not be distinguished from a constant offset.](prior_unseen_children.png){#fig-prior-children .lightbox fig-align="left"}

This is the figure that tests $\tau_1$. Under VG10's constant offset the curves are parallel on the logit scale and **can never cross**, however wide $\tau_{subj}$ is; under a rate they fan, converge and cross. So the qualitative claim this model exists to make is visible in its own prior, and the quantitative question — whether $\text{HalfNormal}(0.5)$ per year puts appreciable mass on trajectories no child could follow, such as a child at the floor or the ceiling for the whole domain — is answerable by eye rather than by argument.

![Nested Beta-Binomial counts for one unseen child per draw: words understood drawn at the child's own $p_U$, then words spoken drawn **conditional on that count**.](prior_unseen_child_counts.png){#fig-prior-child-counts .lightbox fig-align="left"}

The nesting is the point of the second figure. A prior can imply a perfectly reasonable expected trajectory and still put a real administration at an impossible count once the child effect and the dispersion are both in play, and only a count figure can show that.

::: {.callout-note}

The normality tests in this table are reported for completeness. They are not a check on the model: the outcome is a bounded count, which is not expected to be normally distributed, and the model does not assume that it is.

:::

The frame is VG10's, unchanged. What differs is which part of it carries the new information, and the answer is different for a child's own rate than for the population spread of rates. A child's **own** rate is identified only by seeing them more than once, and by how far apart those observations sit; around half the Down syndrome pool has repeated measures and the median repeater is followed for about a year, so the individual rates come from a real longitudinal subset, and a child seen once has theirs shrunk almost entirely to the population. $\tau_1$ is not in that position. Between-child variance at age $a$ is $\tau_0^2 + 2\rho_{01}\tau_0\tau_1 D + \tau_1^2 D^2$, with $D$ the distance from the reference age in years, so a child seen **once** at $D \neq 0$ informs both $\tau_1$ and $\rho_{01}$ through how far they sit from the population curve. Singletons are cross-sectional evidence about the rate spread rather than passengers on it — which is exactly why the age leverage described below is a live concern.

### Prior to posterior {#sec-contraction}

How much each prior was narrowed by the data, computed from this fit's trace rather than read off the figures above.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
from vocab_growth.report_cells import render_prior_posterior_contraction

render_prior_posterior_contraction()
```

The specific risk in this model is a **funnel on $\tau_1$**: a large share of the pool contributes one observation each, so those children's *own* rates are pinned almost entirely by the prior — even though, as above, their distance from the reference age still speaks to $\tau_1$ through the marginal spread. Non-centring and a prior with mass near zero are the mitigations. The signature to watch for is low effective sample size on $\tau_1$ specifically while the rest of the model looks healthy.

A second risk sits on the same parameter and is not about geometry. The rate enters the between-child variance as $\tau_1^2 D^2$, so an observation's weight grows with its distance from the reference age — and the pool's ages are heavily left-massed, with a median of 36 months but a tail to 115. The few dozen spoken observations above 84 months are a few per cent of the rows and carried roughly a third of the cross-sectional information about $\tau_1$ on the 2026-08 frame; on comprehension, a dozen rows carried about a fifth. Because $\tau_1$ is a single global parameter, it sets the between-child spread at *every* age, so leverage sitting in that sparse tail propagates back into the well-populated range this report actually shows. The gate for it is a refit capped at 84 months, checking whether $\tau_1$ moves materially; see [the implementation plan](../../../notes/202608141900-child-slope-implementation-plan.md) §G5b.

## Findings {#sec-findings}

### How much do children differ in their own rate of growth?

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
import pandas as _pd

_d = _pd.read_csv("diagnostics.csv", index_col=0)
_rows = [
    ("Rate spread, comprehension $\\tau_1^{(u)}$", "tau_subj_u_1"),
    ("Rate spread, production ratio $\\tau_1^{(q)}$", "tau_subj_q_1"),
    ("Offset-rate correlation, comprehension", "tau_subj_u_rho"),
    ("Offset-rate correlation, production ratio", "tau_subj_q_rho"),
]
_present = [(label, name) for label, name in _rows if name in _d.index]
if _present:
    print("| Quantity | Posterior mean | SD | 89% ETI | ESS (bulk) | R-hat |")
    print("| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |")
    for label, name in _present:
        r = _d.loc[name]
        print(
            f"| {label} (`{name}`) | {r['mean']:.3f} | {r['sd']:.3f} | "
            f"{r['eti89_lb']:.3f} to {r['eti89_ub']:.3f} | "
            f"{r['ess_bulk']:,.0f} | {r['r_hat']:.3f} |"
        )
    print()
    print(
        ": Read at render time from this fit's own `diagnostics.csv`, so it cannot "
        "drift from the model it describes. Read the two rate spreads as "
        "**magnitudes, not as tests**: `tau_subj_u_1` and `tau_subj_q_1` are "
        "HalfNormal-supported, so their equal-tailed intervals exclude zero by "
        "construction and cannot be evidence that a rate exists. The two "
        "offset-rate correlations are on (-1, 1) with prior mass either side of "
        "zero, so their intervals do carry that meaning."
    )
else:
    print("_This fit's `diagnostics.csv` carries no child-slope rows._")
```

**This is what the model exists to produce**, and under every earlier model in the family both rate spreads are exactly zero by construction.

**Whether a rate exists at all is answered elsewhere, and more weakly than this table looks.** As above, neither $\tau_1$ interval can bear on it. The evidence that does is predictive: refitting with a whole fold of children removed from the likelihood — leave-one-*child*-out rather than leave-one-observation-out — put VG19 **+2.10 SE** above VG10 across the frame's children at the `test` tier, as recorded in the gate record of 2026-08-21. That supports the slope block as a whole, both rates and both offset-rate correlations together. It is not a per-outcome result, and the per-outcome PSIS-LOO margins that once looked like one were leakage: with 1.86 spoken observations per child, leave-one-observation-out was largely scoring each model's ability to predict a child's second visit from their first, which is exactly the comparison four per-child parameters win. Against VG20 on the whole-child criterion the margin was **+0.93 SE** — indistinguishable — on the same record. See [the gate record](../../../notes/202608212000-vg19-gates-g2-g4-g5.md) §4e.

Four qualifications belong with the numbers.

**A rate is not a forecast for a child.** A fitted rate for a child seen twice is mostly prior. These quantities describe how much children in this pool differ from one another in their trajectories; they do not predict an individual's future.

**The two outcomes' rates are not separately trustworthy.** The drift that motivated the block was measured on the spoken proportion, which is the product of comprehension and conversion, so it cannot say which curve owns it; and the predictive evidence above is a single joint margin, not one per outcome. Read them as a pair.

**Neither rate spread is testable from its own interval.** Both are `HalfNormal`-supported, so their equal-tailed intervals exclude zero by construction. The two offset-rate correlations are different — they live on $(-1, 1)$ with prior mass either side of zero, so their intervals do carry evidential weight, and $\tau_1^{(u)}$'s correlation excludes zero only marginally.

**Comprehension and production may honestly differ.** Gate 1 found the comprehension slope worth almost nothing once restricted to children with repeated measures. If $\tau_1^{(u)}$ comes back near zero while $\tau_1^{(q)}$ does not, that is the expected result and not a defect.

### Between-child variation

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
from vocab_growth.report_cells import render_variation_table

render_variation_table()
```

Under a rate, between-child spread is no longer a single number: it is $\sqrt{\tau_0^2 + 2\rho_{01}\tau_0\tau_1 D + \tau_1^2 D^2}$ at $D$ years from the reference age — a parabola in age with its minimum at $D = -\rho_{01}\tau_0/\tau_1$. A negative $\rho_{01}$ places the tightest point in the future and has children fanning out on both sides of it, which is a real qualitative claim the constant-offset model cannot make.

## Limits {#sec-limits}

- **Gated against VG10, not VG20.** VG19 and VG20 are parallel refinements of the same parent and are not composable as written: VG20 estimates one correlation between the two outcomes' constant offsets, VG19 estimates two different ones between each outcome's own offset and rate. Their union is a $4 \times 4$ covariance whose most interesting element — whether children who gain comprehension faster also convert faster — is estimated by neither. This model therefore does **not** carry $\rho_{uq}$, and its child-level intervals are not directly comparable with VG20's.
- **Neither this model nor VG20 is the end of the line, and VG22 is the successor to both.** Each holds half of the same structure — VG19 gives children rates but decouples the two outcomes, VG20 couples them but freezes the spread in age — so the cross-outcome element Gate 1 found strongest, a child's comprehension *level* predicting their production-ratio *rate*, is estimated by neither. The answer is not an unrestricted $4 \times 4$: Gate 1 found that singular at maximum likelihood, with rank 3 reaching the identical likelihood. VG22 is the registered low-rank factor form, with `rank` fitted as a sensitivity family because the residual likelihood cannot choose it. Read the results here as one half of a comparison that VG22's fits will complete ([#233](https://github.com/dseinternational/vocabulary-growth/issues/233), [`notes/202608221000`](../../../notes/202608221000-four-by-four-gate1.md)).
- **A linear rate on the logit scale is a strong extrapolation.** It is constant across the whole 8-115 month domain. If a child's divergence from the population curve is not linear in age, this model reports an average slope and gives no warning that it has done so.
- **Individual rates are identified by a subset; $\tau_1$ is not.** A child observed once has no within-child slope in the data, so their own rate is shrunk to the population and the effective sample for *individual* rates is much smaller than the pool. The population parameter is a different case: a singleton at distance $D$ from the reference age informs $\tau_1$ and $\rho_{01}$ cross-sectionally, through the marginal variance $\tau_0^2 + 2\rho_{01}\tau_0\tau_1 D + \tau_1^2 D^2$. That is what makes the age leverage above matter — the information is real, but it is concentrated in the sparse older tail rather than spread across the pool.
- **It is one pair of numbers for the whole pool.** No study-level or subgroup variation in the rate is estimated, and the pool spans several countries and languages.
- **Nothing here is causal.** Everything reported is an association with age, not an effect of it, and a fitted rate is a description of how this pool's children differ rather than a mechanism.
- **The reference inventory is a harmonisation.** Counts from different checklists are placed on a common 810-word scale; it is a unit of measurement, not an instrument any child sat.
